title: Anti-corruption sanctions: Preparing for the time after Trump – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: The authors argue the next US administration should impose Global Magnitsky Act anti-corruption sanctions from day one against foreign persons who benefited from Trump-era insider deals (in Gaza, Kazakhstan, Bosnia, Central Asia and elsewhere), and that Europeans should start signalling support now to deter further corrupt dealing and prepare coordinated EU-US sanctions and anti-corruption enforcement.

themes.theme: Trump-era insider dealing and its long-term risks

insights.claim: Many Trump administration foreign policy initiatives are structured to make money for people selected by Trump officials, unjustly enriching a chosen few.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: This framing is the article's core allegation and sets up the case for anti-corruption sanctions as a corrective tool once the administration changes—relevant for assessing political/regulatory risk tied to deals struck with Trump-linked entities.
insights.quote: Many—perhaps most—Trump administration foreign policy initiatives find ways to make money for people selected by Trump officials. These deals unjustly enrich a chosen few.

insights.claim: The authors recommend the next US administration introduce anti-corruption sanctions from its first day in office, barring non-US persons or institutions involved in insider transactions from the US and its financial system.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: Day-one sanctions risk is a concrete political-transition scenario for 2028 (or after a Trump exit) that could immediately freeze out foreign parties tied to current Trump-era deals from US markets—material for counterparty due diligence today.
insights.quote: the next US administration should introduce anti-corruption sanctions from its first day in office. The new administration could bar non-US persons or institutions involved in such transactions from the US itself and from the American financial system.
insights.locator: To address this threat to peace

insights.claim: The sanctions tool proposed would rely on the Global Magnitsky Act and related executive orders, including Trump-issued executive order 13818, which authorizes sanctions on foreign persons involved in corruption such as misappropriation of state assets, expropriation of private assets, corrupt government contracting or resource extraction deals, or bribery.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: Executive order 13818 already exists and requires no new legislation, making rapid day-one deployment legally plausible and lowering the barrier to this becoming real policy under a new administration.
insights.quote: Executive order 13818 authorises sanctions against any “foreign person”...who participated in: corruption, including the misappropriation of state assets, the expropriation of private assets for personal gain, corruption related to government contracts or the extraction of natural resources, or bribery
insights.locator: Executive order 13818 authorises sanctions

insights.claim: Europeans can act now, even before a US administration change, by publicly declaring expectations that a future US administration will break from insider-enrichment practices, preserving information about US insider dealing, and refusing to support or finance such deals where European interests are involved, including in the south Caucasus, Western Balkans, Gaza, Russia and Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: European governments and EU-linked financiers are being urged to withhold support from deals tied to Trump-era insiders in these six specific regions now, which could limit financing availability for such projects even before US sanctions materialize.
insights.quote: Over the next two years, Europeans can also preserve information about US insider dealing while publicly refusing to support or finance such deals where European interests are involved, including in the south Caucasus, Western Balkans, Gaza, Russia and Ukraine.
insights.locator: Europeans can help this along even now

insights.claim: Early signalling by American and European leaders now may deter potential foreign partners from entering into corrupt deals with the current administration over its remaining two years.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: The deterrence effect is a near-term lever: credible pre-commitment to future sanctions could cool foreign appetite for entering new Trump-linked insider deals over 2026-2028.
insights.quote: Clear signalling from American and European political leaders now may deter potential foreign partners of the current administration from entering into corrupt deals over the remaining two years of the administration.
insights.locator: Starting discussions about sanctions now

themes.theme: What sanctions can and cannot do

insights.claim: US anti-corruption sanctions under executive order 13818 apply only to non-American citizens, meaning US beneficiaries of insider schemes would not themselves be directly sanctioned.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: This is a structural limitation: US-based insiders remain untouched by the sanctions tool itself, so the practical leverage comes through foreign counterparties being cut off, not domestic prosecution.
insights.quote: American sanctions apply only to non-American citizens.
insights.locator: American sanctions apply only to non-American

insights.claim: By the end of the Trump administration, many insiders and possibly some foreign persons are likely to be covered by presidential pardons, which could make US criminal investigations difficult or impossible without extensive litigation.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: Anticipated pardons mean criminal prosecution is unlikely to be the enforcement mechanism against Trump-era insider deals; sanctions are framed as the more durable tool precisely because they sidestep the pardon power.
insights.quote: by the end of the Trump administration, many insiders (and possibly some foreign persons) are likely to be covered by presidential pardons. This could make it difficult, if not impossible, to proceed with US criminal investigations

insights.claim: Sanctions are not subject to the presidential pardon power, and their focus on non-US persons and institutions gives them some protection against being framed as part of a partisan agenda.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: This is the authors' central argument for why sanctions, not prosecution, are the more resilient tool for a new administration to unwind Trump-era insider enrichment.
insights.quote: Crucially, sanctions are not subject to the pardon power, and their emphasis on non-US persons and institutions will provide some protection against charges that they are part of a partisan agenda.

themes.theme: Europe's coordinating role and political risks

insights.claim: If jurisdictions like the EU and Britain join new American sanctions efforts, the costs to affected non-US individuals and institutions would be real, and the EU could use bodies like OLAF or the European Public Prosecutor's Office to work alongside US sanctions authorities.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: Coordinated EU-UK-US sanctions would meaningfully raise the cost and reach of enforcement versus US action alone, making joint EU institutional involvement (OLAF, EPPO) a key variable for how effective this sanctions regime could become.
insights.quote: If other jurisdictions like the EU and Britain join new American sanctions efforts, the costs to the non-US individuals and institutions affected will be real.

insights.claim: The EU could propose that it and the US return to coordinating assistance programmes to reinforce public procurement reforms, and more European states should consider adopting national anti-corruption sanctions programmes.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: This is a concrete policy ask for European governments: expand national anti-corruption sanctions regimes and restart EU-US procurement-reform coordination, both trackable legislative developments.
insights.quote: Various European states have national anti-corruption sanctions programmes; more should consider adopting them.

insights.claim: Some may worry that rapid deployment of sanctions could distract from a new administration's positive agenda, but the authors argue this is a false choice since breaking from Trump-era insider dealing should itself be part of a positive governing plan.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: The authors preempt a likely political objection (sanctions as distraction), framing anti-corruption action as complementary to, not competing with, a new administration's broader agenda—useful for gauging how contested this policy proposal might be politically.
insights.quote: Europeans can help make clear that they regard this as a false choice: a break from the insider dealing of the Trump administration should be part of a new, positive plan for government.

insights.claim: Not every example of alleged insider dealing will be proven corrupt, some potential sanctions targets may be important to other administration initiatives, and other countries may object to having their institutions or citizens named in sanctions documents—creating difficult trade-offs for a new administration.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: This is an explicit risk caveat: sanctions targeting will involve contested evidentiary and diplomatic trade-offs, meaning implementation could be slower or narrower than the day-one ideal the authors propose.

insights.claim: The authors cite the view that democratic transitions after corrupt regimes can only achieve two of three goals—being quick, effective and legal—but argue sanctions could get a new US administration closer to achieving all three by providing a fast, legal tool that avoids targeting US citizens while retaining flexibility to adjust.
insights.speaker: Sarah McCool, Jim O’Brien
insights.so_what: This is the article's closing thesis and strongest conviction claim: sanctions are positioned as a uniquely effective, legally durable, and fast tool for a post-Trump administration to unwind insider enrichment, which frames the entire policy recommendation's stakes.
insights.quote: Wise observers of democratic transitions have said that democrats taking power after corrupt regimes should seek to be quick, effective and legal; but that they can be only two of the three. But sanctions might get a new administration closer to three out of three.
insights.locator: Wise observers of democratic transitions
